subChunks.title: 1D Arrays: Declaration, Access & Iteration
subChunks.hookHtml: A single rune is powerful. A sequence of runes, each precisely positioned, is a spell. Arrays are Java's way of storing ordered collections of values under a single name.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Declaring and Creating Arrays

An array holds a fixed number of elements of the same type. You declare and create it in one step:

int[] scores = new int[5];        // 5 ints, all initialised to 0
String[] names = new String[3];   // 3 Strings, all null
double[] prices = {9.99, 14.50, 3.25}; // array literal — size inferred

The size is fixed at creation time and cannot be changed later.

Accessing Elements

Array indices start at 0. The last valid index is length - 1:

int[] mana = {40, 80, 120};
System.out.println(mana[0]);  // 40 — first element
System.out.println(mana[2]);  // 120 — last element
// mana[3] would throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException

Array Length

array.length (not a method call — no parentheses) gives the number of elements:

System.out.println(mana.length);  // 3

Iterating Over Arrays

The classic for loop uses an index counter:

for (int i = 0; i < mana.length; i++) {
    System.out.println(mana[i]);
}

The enhanced for loop (for-each) is simpler when you don't need the index:

for (int value : mana) {
    System.out.println(value);
}

Common Array Operations

// Sum all elements
int total = 0;
for (int v : mana) total += v;

// Find maximum
int max = mana[0];
for (int v : mana) {
    if (v > max) max = v;
}

// Check if an element exists
boolean found = false;
for (int v : mana) {
    if (v == 80) { found = true; break; }
}

Default Values

When you create an array with new, elements are set to type defaults: 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, and null for reference types (including String).

storyBeats.text: The Academy's potion lab has rows of numbered vials, each labelled and arranged in a precise sequence. The head alchemist reaches for vial seven without looking. He knows exactly where it is.

storyBeats.speaker: Head Alchemist Corda
storyBeats.text: An array is a rack of numbered vials. You ask for vial zero, you get the first one. Ask for vial four, you get the fifth. The first slot is always zero — programmers count from zero, not one. Get used to it now; the alternative is a lifetime of off-by-one errors.

storyBeats.speaker: Head Alchemist Corda
storyBeats.text: The rack has a fixed number of slots. You cannot add a sixth slot without building a new rack. Arrays are immutable in size. If you ask for slot five on a five-element array, Java throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. It is one of the most common runtime errors you will encounter.

storyBeats.speaker: Head Alchemist Corda
storyBeats.text: To inspect every vial in sequence, you iterate. Two ways: the indexed for loop (when you need the slot number) and the enhanced for-each loop (when you only care about the contents). Both are correct. Choose based on whether you need the index.

storyBeats.speaker: Sum of all potion strengths

storyBeats.text: Corda pours every vial into a single flask, counts them without hesitation, and seals it. 'Iterate, accumulate, verify. That is the array mindset.'

learningObjectives: Declare and initialise a 1D array using both new[] and an array literal
Access array elements by index and explain zero-based indexing
Use array.length to iterate safely without going out of bounds
Implement common array operations: sum, maximum, element search
commonMistakes: Using array.length as the last valid index — the last index is length-1
Writing array.length() with parentheses — length is a field, not a method
Forgetting that int[] defaults to 0 and String[] defaults to null after new[]
Modifying the loop variable in a for-each — it is a copy, not a reference to the slot
assessmentCriteria: Can declare, initialise, and iterate over a 1D array without going out of bounds
Can compute the sum and maximum value of an integer array
Can explain what ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException means and how to prevent it
Can choose correctly between an indexed for loop and a for-each loop
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what a Java array is, why indices start at 0, and what happens if you access index array.length instead of array.length-1. Use a physical analogy to make it memorable.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
The Academy's mana monitoring system reads six sensor readings into an array. Your task:

  1. Declare and initialise: int[] readings = {42, 75, 13, 88, 56, 31}
  2. Print the first and last element
  3. Compute and print the sum of all elements
  4. Find and print the maximum value
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
From scratch: declare int[] spellPowers = {10, 45, 23, 67, 34, 89, 12}. Then:

  • Print the element at index 3

  • Print the minimum value (smallest element)

questions.questionHtml: What is the index of the last element in an array with 6 elements?
questions.explanationHtml: Arrays use zero-based indexing. A 6-element array has valid indices 0 through 5. Index 6 does not exist and would throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

questions.questionHtml: This code throws an exception at runtime. Why?
questions.correctAnswer: The loop condition should be i < arr.length, not i <= arr.length — the last iteration accesses arr[4] which does not exist
questions.explanationHtml: A 4-element array has indices 0–3. Using i <= arr.length includes i = 4, which causes ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Always use i < arr.length.

questions.questionHtml: array.length is called with parentheses, like a method.
questions.explanationHtml: length is a public final field on arrays, not a method. You access it as array.length with no parentheses. (Contrast with String.length() which IS a method.)

subChunks.title: 2D Arrays & Array Utilities
subChunks.hookHtml: The magical ward grid covers a fortress in a five-by-five pattern. Each cell holds a power level. To traverse it systematically — row by row, column by column — you need a two-dimensional array.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
2D Arrays

A 2D array is an array of arrays. You think of it as a grid with rows and columns:

int[][] grid = new int[3][4];  // 3 rows, 4 columns
// Or with a literal:
int[][] matrix = {
    {1, 2, 3},
    {4, 5, 6},
    {7, 8, 9}
};

Access with two indices — matrix[row][col]:

System.out.println(matrix[1][2]);  // 6 (row 1, col 2)

Iterating Over a 2D Array

for (int row = 0; row < matrix.length; row++) {
    for (int col = 0; col < matrix[row].length; col++) {
        System.out.print(matrix[row][col] + " ");
    }
    System.out.println();
}

Arrays Utility Class

java.util.Arrays provides helpful static methods:

import java.util.Arrays;

int[] nums = {5, 3, 8, 1, 9};
Arrays.sort(nums);                   // sorts in place: [1,3,5,8,9]
System.out.println(Arrays.toString(nums)); // prints: [1, 3, 5, 8, 9]
int[] copy = Arrays.copyOf(nums, 3); // first 3 elements: [1,3,5]

Arrays.toString() is especially handy — printing an array directly gives a useless memory address ([I@3764951d), but Arrays.toString() gives a readable format.

storyBeats.text: The Academy's ward-mapping chamber displays a glowing grid on the stone floor. Each square cell pulses with a different intensity. A junior ward-keeper is trying to inspect every cell by walking in a random pattern and losing count.

storyBeats.speaker: Ward-Keeper Mira
storyBeats.text: A two-dimensional array is exactly what it sounds like: rows and columns. You access a cell with two indices — row first, then column. grid[2][3] is row two, column three.

storyBeats.speaker: Ward-Keeper Mira
storyBeats.text: To inspect every cell, nest two loops: an outer loop over rows, an inner loop over columns. The outer loop uses grid.length for the row count. The inner loop uses grid[row].length for the column count — because in Java, each row is its own array, and rows can theoretically have different lengths.

storyBeats.speaker: Ward-Keeper Mira
storyBeats.text: One more essential tool: Arrays.toString(). If you print an array directly, Java gives you a useless memory address. Import java.util.Arrays and use Arrays.toString() to see the actual values. And Arrays.sort() to sort in place — no extra code needed.

learningObjectives: Declare and initialise a 2D array using both new[][] and a nested literal
Iterate over a 2D array using nested for loops
Use Arrays.sort() and Arrays.toString() from java.util.Arrays
commonMistakes: Reversing row and column when accessing 2D array elements
Printing an array directly — always use Arrays.toString() or iterate
Forgetting to import java.util.Arrays before using Arrays.sort() or Arrays.toString()
Using matrix.length for both loops — the inner loop should use matrix[row].length
assessmentCriteria: Can declare, populate, and print all elements of a 2D array using nested loops
Can access a specific cell by row and column index
Can sort a 1D array and print it in readable form using java.util.Arrays
Can explain why printing an array directly does not show its contents
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain 2D arrays using a grid analogy. How do you declare one, access a specific cell, and iterate over all cells? Why does Java require nested loops?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
You have a 3×3 magic square grid. Your tasks:

  1. Declare int[][] grid = {{2,7,6},{9,5,1},{4,3,8}}
  2. Print the element at row 1, col 2 (should be 1)
  3. Use nested loops to compute and print the sum of all elements
  4. Declare int[] powers = {15, 3, 42, 8, 27}, sort it, and print it using Arrays.toString()
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From scratch: declare a 2×4 integer grid with any values. Print each row on its own line (space-separated). Then print the largest value in the entire grid. Finally create and sort int[] vals = {88, 12, 45, 67, 3, 99} and print it with Arrays.toString().

questions.explanationHtml: m[2] is the third row {5,6}. m[2][1] is the second element of that row: 6.

questions.questionHtml: A developer writes System.out.println(myArray);. What will likely be printed?
options: The contents of the array, comma-separated
questions.explanationHtml: Arrays don't override toString(), so printing one directly shows the type prefix ([I for int array) followed by the object's hashcode. Use Arrays.toString(myArray) to see the actual values.
